0.2 Course Voice
The chapters use neutral course language rather than references to a specific university, term, or software stack. Each chapter emphasizes concepts, reproducible code, and statistical judgment.

title: 2  Statistical Learning Foundations
text:
2.1 Learning Objectives
Statistical learning is the study of using data to estimate structure, make predictions, and quantify uncertainty. The course begins with a single guiding idea: every method is trying to learn something about an unknown relationship between inputs and an outcome.

title: 2  Statistical Learning Foundations
text:
Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, regression, and classification problems.
Separate prediction goals from inference goals.
Define reducible error, irreducible error, training error, and test error.
Describe the main parts of a reproducible statistical learning workflow.
Inspect a data set before fitting a first model.

title: 2  Statistical Learning Foundations
text:
2.2 The Statistical Learning Problem
For a response variable Y and predictors X = (X_1,\ldots,X_p), the regression function is

f(x) = \operatorname{E}(Y \mid X = x).

The observed response can be written as

Y = f(X) + \epsilon,

where \epsilon collects the part of the outcome that cannot be predicted from the available predictors. A fitted model \hat f is an estimate of f. Some methods estimate a very simple surface, such as a line or plane. Others estimate a highly flexible surface, such as a tree ensemble or kernel classifier. The question is not which method is universally best; the question is which method learns useful structure for the task at hand.
In supervised learning, the data include an outcome. Regression predicts a quantitative outcome; classification predicts a class label or class probability. In unsupervised learning, there is no designated outcome. The goal is to find structure among observations or variables, such as clusters, low-dimensional representations, or unusual observations.

title: 2  Statistical Learning Foundations
text:
2.3 Prediction and Inference
Prediction asks for accurate values of \hat Y on future or held-out cases. Inference asks what the data suggest about the relationship between variables. The same fitted model can be used for both, but the emphasis changes:








Goal
Main question
Typical evidence




Prediction
How well does the model generalize?
Validation error, test error, calibration


Inference
Which relationships are supported?
Coefficients, uncertainty intervals, diagnostics


Description
What patterns are visible?
Summaries, plots, cluster profiles


Decision support
What action should be taken?
Error costs, uncertainty, constraints



A model that predicts well is not automatically interpretable. A model with clean coefficient interpretations is not automatically the best predictor. Students should name the goal before comparing models.

title: 2  Statistical Learning Foundations
text:
2.4 Error and Generalization
At a new point x_0, prediction error has two parts:

\operatorname{E}\{(Y - \hat f(x_0))^2\}
= \operatorname{E}\{(f(x_0) - \hat f(x_0))^2\}
+ \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon).

The first term is reducible because better data, better features, or a better method may lower it. The second term is irreducible because two observations with the same predictors can still have different outcomes.
Training error is computed on the data used to fit the model. Test error is computed on data not used in fitting or tuning. Flexible models can drive training error down while increasing test error, so training error alone is not enough evidence of a useful model.

title: 2  Statistical Learning Foundations
text:
2.5 Boston Housing Opening Analysis
A first analysis should begin before modeling. In the Boston housing data, the observational unit is a census tract, the response medv is median home value, and candidate predictors include crime rate, industrial land use, distance to employment centers, pupil-teacher ratio, and other tract-level summaries.
The opening analysis should answer five questions:

What is the response, and what does one row represent?
Which predictors are quantitative and which are categorical or binary?
Are there unusual values, impossible values, or strong skew?
Which pairwise relationships with the response are most visible?
Which baseline model is simple enough to interpret?


RPython



library(MASS)

data(Boston)
summary(Boston)
pairs(Boston[, c("medv", "lstat", "rm", "ptratio", "crim")])

baseline <- lm(medv ~ lstat, data = Boston)
expanded <- lm(medv ~ lstat + rm + ptratio + crim, data = Boston)
summary(baseline)
summary(expanded)




import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_california_housing
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

housing = fetch_california_housing(as_frame=True).frame
housing = housing.rename(columns={"MedHouseVal": "medv"})

print(housing.describe())
pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(
    housing[["medv", "MedInc", "AveRooms", "HouseAge", "AveOccup"]],
    figsize=(8, 8)
)
plt.show()

baseline = smf.ols("medv ~ MedInc", data=housing).fit()
expanded = smf.ols(
    "medv ~ MedInc + AveRooms + HouseAge + AveOccup",
    data=housing
).fit()

print(baseline.summary())
print(expanded.summary())




The purpose of this first fit is orientation. A strong association between lstat and medv suggests a useful baseline, while the expanded model shows how additional predictors can improve prediction and change interpretation.

title: 2  Statistical Learning Foundations
text:
2.6 Assumptions as Modeling Questions
Ordinary least squares relies on assumptions that should be treated as diagnostic questions rather than as boxes to check mechanically:







Assumption
Practical question




Linearity
Is the conditional mean roughly linear in the predictors used?


Independent errors
Are observations collected in a way that creates dependence?


Constant variance
Does residual spread change with fitted values or predictors?


Approximate normality
Are interval estimates relying on a poor error approximation?


No extreme leverage
Are a few observations controlling the fitted relationship?



The assumptions matter because they affect interpretation, uncertainty, and prediction. When a diagnostic reveals a problem, the next step may be a transformation, an interaction, a nonlinear term, a different model class, or a narrower claim.

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:
3.1 Learning Objectives
Linear regression is the first complete statistical learning workflow: specification, estimation, interpretation, diagnostics, uncertainty, and prediction. It is simple enough to study carefully and rich enough to introduce most habits used throughout the course.

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:
3.2 Least Squares Regression
The multiple linear regression model has the form

Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_pX_{ip}
+ \epsilon_i.

Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients that minimize residual sum of squares:

\hat{\beta} =
\arg\min_{\beta}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2.

The fitted value is \hat y_i = x_i^\top\hat\beta, and the residual is e_i = y_i - \hat y_i. A coefficient estimates the expected change in the response for a one-unit increase in that predictor, holding the other predictors in the model fixed. That “holding fixed” phrase is essential: coefficient meaning depends on the full model specification.

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:
3.3 Advertising Model Sequence
The advertising data provide a compact way to move from simple regression to multiple regression. Suppose sales is the response and TV, radio, and newspaper are advertising budgets.

RPython



set.seed(571)
advertising <- data.frame(
  TV = runif(200, 0, 300),
  radio = runif(200, 0, 50),
  newspaper = runif(200, 0, 100)
)
advertising$sales <- 3 +
  0.045 * advertising$TV +
  0.19 * advertising$radio +
  0.002 * advertising$TV * advertising$radio +
  rnorm(200, sd = 2)

tv_fit <- lm(sales ~ TV, data = advertising)
media_fit <- lm(sales ~ TV + radio + newspaper, data = advertising)
interaction_fit <- lm(sales ~ TV * radio + newspaper, data = advertising)

summary(tv_fit)
summary(media_fit)
summary(interaction_fit)




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
advertising = pd.DataFrame({
    "TV": rng.uniform(0, 300, 200),
    "radio": rng.uniform(0, 50, 200),
    "newspaper": rng.uniform(0, 100, 200),
})
advertising["sales"] = (
    3
    + 0.045 * advertising["TV"]
    + 0.19 * advertising["radio"]
    + 0.002 * advertising["TV"] * advertising["radio"]
    + rng.normal(0, 2, 200)
)

tv_fit = smf.ols("sales ~ TV", data=advertising).fit()
media_fit = smf.ols("sales ~ TV + radio + newspaper", data=advertising).fit()
interaction_fit = smf.ols(
    "sales ~ TV * radio + newspaper",
    data=advertising
).fit()

print(tv_fit.summary())
print(media_fit.summary())
print(interaction_fit.summary())




The simple model asks whether TV budget alone predicts sales. The multiple regression model asks whether each medium explains variation after accounting for the others. The interaction model asks whether the effect of one medium changes as another medium changes.

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:
3.4 Train/Test Evaluation
Regression teaching often begins with coefficient tables, but prediction requires held-out evaluation. Split before comparing candidate models:

RPython



set.seed(571)
id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(advertising)), size = 0.8 * nrow(advertising))
train <- advertising[id, ]
test <- advertising[-id, ]

fit <- lm(sales ~ TV + radio + newspaper, data = train)
pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test)

rmse <- sqrt(mean((test$sales - pred)^2))
test_r2 <- 1 - sum((test$sales - pred)^2) /
  sum((test$sales - mean(test$sales))^2)




from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

train, test = train_test_split(
    advertising,
    train_size=0.8,
    random_state=571
)

fit = smf.ols("sales ~ TV + radio + newspaper", data=train).fit()
pred = fit.predict(test)

rmse = mean_squared_error(test["sales"], pred) ** 0.5
test_r2 = r2_score(test["sales"], pred)

print({"rmse": rmse, "test_r2": test_r2})




Residual standard error describes typical residual size in the training data. Test RMSE describes typical prediction error on observations not used to estimate the coefficients. Both can be useful, but they answer different questions.

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:
3.5 Interactions and Marginal Effects
An interaction lets the effect of one predictor depend on another:

\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X,Z)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1X + \beta_2Z + \beta_3XZ.

The marginal effect of X is

\frac{\partial \operatorname{E}(Y \mid X,Z)}{\partial X}
= \beta_1 + \beta_3Z.

After an interaction is included, the main effect of X is the effect when Z=0. If Z=0 is not meaningful, centering Z can make the main effect easier to interpret.

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:
3.6 Diagnostics and Influence
Diagnostics convert assumptions into visible questions:







Diagnostic
Question




Residuals vs. fitted values
Is the mean structure missing curvature or interactions?


Scale-location plot
Does residual spread change across fitted values?


Normal Q-Q plot
Are uncertainty summaries sensitive to tail behavior?


Leverage
Are some predictor combinations unusual?


Cook’s distance
Are individual observations strongly changing the fit?


Correlation or VIF
Are coefficients unstable because predictors overlap?




RPython



par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit)




import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as stats

residuals = fit.resid
fitted = fit.fittedvalues

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axes[0].scatter(fitted, residuals)
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Fitted values")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residuals")
stats.probplot(residuals, dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




The goal is not to make every plot perfect. The goal is to notice model-data disagreement and decide whether it changes the claim.

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:
3.7 Coefficient Interpretation
Good interpretation follows a stable template:

name the response scale,
name the predictor and unit change,
state the direction and magnitude,
state what is held fixed,
avoid causal language unless the design supports it.

For example: holding radio and newspaper budgets fixed, an additional unit of TV advertising budget is associated with an estimated increase of \hat\beta_1 sales units. This is an association from an observational regression, not by itself proof that changing TV spending would cause the same change in sales.

title: 3  Linear Regression
text:
3.8 Chapter Synthesis
Fit simple, multiple, and interaction regression models to the same data set. Compare coefficient interpretations, residual standard error, test RMSE, and a predicted-versus-actual plot. End with a paragraph explaining which predictors matter, whether the interaction is useful, and whether the model is more valuable for prediction or inference.

title: 4  Interactions and Marginal Effects
text:
4.1 Learning Objectives
Interactions are the first place where a regression model stops being a collection of independent additive effects. They let the relationship between one predictor and the response depend on another predictor.

title: 4  Interactions and Marginal Effects
text:
Write a regression model with an interaction term.
Interpret main effects when an interaction is present.
Compute marginal effects for binary-continuous and continuous-continuous interactions.
Use plots to communicate conditional relationships.
Explain why interactions should be motivated by the question and checked against the data.

title: 4  Interactions and Marginal Effects
text:
4.2 Interaction Model
For two predictors X and Z, an interaction model is

\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X,Z)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1X + \beta_2Z + \beta_3XZ.

The coefficient \beta_3 says how the slope of X changes as Z changes. The marginal effect of X is

\frac{\partial \operatorname{E}(Y \mid X,Z)}{\partial X}
= \beta_1 + \beta_3Z.

The main effect \beta_1 is therefore the effect of X when Z=0. If Z=0 is not substantively meaningful, centering Z makes the main effect easier to explain.

title: 4  Interactions and Marginal Effects
text:
4.3 Binary by Continuous Interaction
Suppose the return to advertising differs by whether a campaign is digital-first. The model includes a continuous predictor, a binary indicator, and their product.

RPython



set.seed(571)
n <- 250
campaign <- data.frame(
  spend = runif(n, 10, 100),
  digital = rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.45)
)
campaign$sales <- 20 + 0.55 * campaign$spend +
  7 * campaign$digital +
  0.35 * campaign$spend * campaign$digital +
  rnorm(n, sd = 8)

fit_interaction <- lm(sales ~ spend * digital, data = campaign)
summary(fit_interaction)




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
n = 250
campaign = pd.DataFrame({
    "spend": rng.uniform(10, 100, n),
    "digital": rng.binomial(1, 0.45, n)
})
campaign["sales"] = (
    20 + 0.55 * campaign["spend"] +
    7 * campaign["digital"] +
    0.35 * campaign["spend"] * campaign["digital"] +
    rng.normal(0, 8, n)
)

fit_interaction = smf.ols("sales ~ spend * digital", data=campaign).fit()
print(fit_interaction.summary())




The slope for non-digital campaigns is \beta_1. The slope for digital-first campaigns is \beta_1+\beta_3. The intercept difference is not the whole story because the gap between groups changes with spending.

title: 4  Interactions and Marginal Effects
text:
4.4 Continuous by Continuous Interaction
When both predictors are continuous, the effect of each predictor is a function of the other. A coefficient table alone is rarely enough. Use predicted values over a grid of meaningful values.

RPython



new_grid <- expand.grid(
  spend = seq(10, 100, length.out = 50),
  digital = c(0, 1)
)
new_grid$predicted_sales <- predict(fit_interaction, newdata = new_grid)
head(new_grid)




new_grid = pd.DataFrame({
    "spend": np.tile(np.linspace(10, 100, 50), 2),
    "digital": np.repeat([0, 1], 50)
})
new_grid["predicted_sales"] = fit_interaction.predict(new_grid)
print(new_grid.head())




This prediction-grid approach also works for interactions between income and age, education and experience, price and promotion, or any other pair where the substantive effect is conditional.

title: 4  Interactions and Marginal Effects
text:
4.5 Standard Errors for Marginal Effects
For a continuous-continuous interaction, the marginal effect \beta_1+\beta_3Z has uncertainty because it depends on two estimated coefficients. Its variance is

\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1 + z\hat\beta_3)
= \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)
+ z^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_3)
+ 2z\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_3).

The uncertainty can be narrow in some regions of Z and wide in others. This is why marginal-effect plots are often more honest than a single starred interaction coefficient.

text:
4.6 Chapter Synthesis
Fit an interaction model, compute predicted values for meaningful combinations of the interacting variables, and explain the result in terms of conditional effects. Avoid saying that a main effect is “positive” or “negative” without stating the value of the interacting variable.

title: 5  Classification Foundations
text:
5.1 Learning Objectives
Classification problems ask for class labels, class probabilities, or ranked risk scores. Before fitting logistic regression, discriminant analysis, trees, or support vector machines, students need a common language for probability, thresholds, and error costs.

title: 5  Classification Foundations
text:
Distinguish class labels from class probabilities.
Explain Bayes’ rule and decision boundaries.
Build and interpret a confusion matrix.
Define sensitivity, specificity, precision, and accuracy.
Explain how thresholds encode decision costs.

title: 5  Classification Foundations
text:
5.2 Class Probabilities and Labels
A classifier often estimates

p_k(x) = \Pr(Y=k \mid X=x)

for each class k. A label is then assigned by a rule, such as choosing the class with the largest estimated probability. In a binary problem, the rule is often

\hat y =
\begin{cases}
1, & \hat p(x) \geq c,\\
0, & \hat p(x) < c.
\end{cases}

The threshold c is a decision choice, not a law of nature.

title: 5  Classification Foundations
text:
5.3 A First Classification Example
The example below creates a two-class data set, estimates a simple probability model, and converts probabilities into labels.

RPython



set.seed(571)
n <- 300
classification_data <- data.frame(
  balance = rnorm(n, mean = 1200, sd = 450),
  income = rnorm(n, mean = 55000, sd = 15000)
)
eta <- -5 + 0.003 * classification_data$balance -
  0.00001 * classification_data$income
classification_data$default <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(eta))

first_model <- glm(default ~ balance + income,
                   data = classification_data,
                   family = binomial)
classification_data$prob <- predict(first_model, type = "response")
classification_data$pred <- ifelse(classification_data$prob >= 0.5, 1, 0)
table(predicted = classification_data$pred,
      observed = classification_data$default)




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
n = 300
classification_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "balance": rng.normal(1200, 450, n),
    "income": rng.normal(55000, 15000, n)
})
eta = -5 + 0.003 * classification_data["balance"] - 0.00001 * classification_data["income"]
prob = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta))
classification_data["default"] = rng.binomial(1, prob)

first_model = smf.logit("default ~ balance + income", data=classification_data).fit()
classification_data["prob"] = first_model.predict(classification_data)
classification_data["pred"] = (classification_data["prob"] >= 0.5).astype(int)
print(pd.crosstab(classification_data["pred"], classification_data["default"]))

title: 5  Classification Foundations
text:
5.4 Confusion Matrix Measures
For a binary classifier:








Measure
Definition
Question




Accuracy
(TP+TN)/(TP+FP+TN+FN)
What fraction of labels are correct?


Sensitivity
TP/(TP+FN)
What fraction of positives are detected?


Specificity
TN/(TN+FP)
What fraction of negatives are rejected?


Precision
TP/(TP+FP)
Among predicted positives, how many are true positives?


False positive rate
FP/(FP+TN)
What fraction of negatives are incorrectly flagged?



No single measure is always best. Rare-event classification often requires sensitivity, specificity, precision, and calibration, not just accuracy.

title: 5  Classification Foundations
text:
5.5 Thresholds and Costs
If false negatives are costly, lower the threshold to catch more positives. If false positives are costly, raise the threshold. The model estimates probability; the threshold translates probability into an action.

title: 5  Classification Foundations
text:
5.6 Chapter Synthesis
Fit a simple classifier, produce predicted probabilities, compare at least two thresholds, and report the resulting confusion matrices. End by explaining which error type matters most for the decision.

title: 6  Logistic Regression and ROC Analysis
text:
6.2 The Logistic Model
For a binary outcome,

p(x) = \Pr(Y=1 \mid X=x).

Logistic regression models the log odds:

\log\left(\frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}\right)
= \beta_0 + x^\top\beta.

The inverse-logit transformation returns the probability:

p(x) =
\frac{\exp(\beta_0+x^\top\beta)}
{1+\exp(\beta_0+x^\top\beta)}.
crumbs: 6  Logistic Regression and ROC Analysis

title: 6  Logistic Regression and ROC Analysis
text:
6.3 Credit Risk Example
Credit-risk modeling makes three ideas visible: rare events, probability estimation, and threshold choice.

RPython



set.seed(571)
n <- 1000
credit <- data.frame(
  balance = rgamma(n, shape = 4, scale = 350),
  income = rnorm(n, mean = 60000, sd = 18000),
  age = round(rnorm(n, mean = 45, sd = 12))
)
eta <- -6 + 0.0032 * credit$balance -
  0.000012 * credit$income - 0.015 * credit$age
credit$default <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(eta))

logit_fit <- glm(default ~ balance + income + age,
                 data = credit,
                 family = binomial)
credit$prob_default <- predict(logit_fit, type = "response")
summary(logit_fit)
exp(coef(logit_fit))




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
n = 1000
credit = pd.DataFrame({
    "balance": rng.gamma(shape=4, scale=350, size=n),
    "income": rng.normal(60000, 18000, n),
    "age": np.round(rng.normal(45, 12, n))
})
eta = -6 + 0.0032 * credit["balance"] - 0.000012 * credit["income"] - 0.015 * credit["age"]
credit["default"] = rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta)))

logit_fit = smf.logit("default ~ balance + income + age", data=credit).fit()
credit["prob_default"] = logit_fit.predict(credit)
print(logit_fit.summary())
print(np.exp(logit_fit.params))




An odds ratio above 1 increases odds of default; an odds ratio below 1 decreases odds, holding other predictors fixed. Probability changes are not constant because the logit curve is nonlinear.

title: 6  Logistic Regression and ROC Analysis
text:
6.4 Binning and Default Rates
Binning a continuous predictor can reveal whether observed risk changes monotonically with the predictor.

RPython



credit$balance_bin <- cut(credit$balance,
                          breaks = quantile(credit$balance, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.1)),
                          include.lowest = TRUE)
aggregate(default ~ balance_bin, data = credit, mean)




credit["balance_bin"] = pd.qcut(credit["balance"], q=10, duplicates="drop")
print(credit.groupby("balance_bin")["default"].mean())




Binning is not a replacement for modeling, but it is a useful diagnostic for risk monotonicity and communication.

title: 6  Logistic Regression and ROC Analysis
text:
6.5 ROC and AUC
An ROC curve plots sensitivity against the false positive rate across all possible thresholds. AUC summarizes how well the model ranks positive cases above negative cases.

RPython



thresholds <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 101)
roc_points <- do.call(rbind, lapply(thresholds, function(cutoff) {
  pred <- ifelse(credit$prob_default >= cutoff, 1, 0)
  tp <- sum(pred == 1 & credit$default == 1)
  fp <- sum(pred == 1 & credit$default == 0)
  tn <- sum(pred == 0 & credit$default == 0)
  fn <- sum(pred == 0 & credit$default == 1)
  data.frame(
    threshold = cutoff,
    sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn),
    false_positive_rate = fp / (fp + tn)
  )
}))
head(roc_points)




thresholds = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
records = []
for cutoff in thresholds:
    pred = (credit["prob_default"] >= cutoff).astype(int)
    tp = ((pred == 1) & (credit["default"] == 1)).sum()
    fp = ((pred == 1) & (credit["default"] == 0)).sum()
    tn = ((pred == 0) & (credit["default"] == 0)).sum()
    fn = ((pred == 0) & (credit["default"] == 1)).sum()
    records.append({
        "threshold": cutoff,
        "sensitivity": tp / (tp + fn),
        "false_positive_rate": fp / (fp + tn)
    })
roc_points = pd.DataFrame(records)
print(roc_points.head())




ROC curves describe ranking performance, not calibration. A model can rank cases well while producing probabilities that are too high or too low.

title: 7  Discriminant Analysis
text:
7.1 Learning Objectives
Discriminant analysis is a probability-based approach to classification. Instead of modeling \Pr(Y=1 \mid X) directly, it models the distribution of predictors within each class and combines those distributions with class priors.

title: 7  Discriminant Analysis
text:
7.2 Bayes’ Rule for Classification
For class k,

\Pr(Y=k \mid X=x)
= \frac{\pi_k f_k(x)}
{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\pi_\ell f_\ell(x)},

where \pi_k is the prior probability of class k and f_k(x) is the class-conditional density.
LDA assumes all classes share a covariance matrix. QDA allows each class to have its own covariance matrix.

title: 7  Discriminant Analysis
text:
7.3 LDA and QDA Example

RPython



library(MASS)

set.seed(571)
n <- 400
disc <- data.frame(
  balance = rnorm(n, 1200, 450),
  income = rnorm(n, 60000, 18000)
)
eta <- -5 + 0.003 * disc$balance - 0.00001 * disc$income
disc$default <- factor(rbinom(n, 1, plogis(eta)),
                       labels = c("No", "Yes"))

lda_fit <- lda(default ~ balance + income, data = disc)
qda_fit <- qda(default ~ balance + income, data = disc)

lda_prob <- predict(lda_fit)$posterior[, "Yes"]
qda_prob <- predict(qda_fit)$posterior[, "Yes"]
head(lda_prob)




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
n = 400
disc = pd.DataFrame({
    "balance": rng.normal(1200, 450, n),
    "income": rng.normal(60000, 18000, n)
})
eta = -5 + 0.003 * disc["balance"] - 0.00001 * disc["income"]
disc["default"] = np.where(rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta))), "Yes", "No")

X = disc[["balance", "income"]]
y = disc["default"]
lda_fit = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X, y)
qda_fit = QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X, y)

lda_prob = lda_fit.predict_proba(X)[:, list(lda_fit.classes_).index("Yes")]
qda_prob = qda_fit.predict_proba(X)[:, list(qda_fit.classes_).index("Yes")]
print(lda_prob[:5])




LDA is more restrictive but often more stable. QDA is more flexible but requires more data because it estimates separate covariance structures.

title: 8  Model Assessment and Resampling
text:
8.1 Learning Objectives
Resampling methods turn model fitting into model evaluation. Instead of trusting one fitted model or one arbitrary train/test split, we repeatedly refit a model on related versions of the data and study how its predictions or estimates change. This chapter uses resampling to answer two practical questions: how well will a model predict new data, and how much uncertainty is attached to a fitted statistic or model coefficient?

text:

title: 8  Model Assessment and Resampling
section: 8.2 Why Training Error Is Not Enough
text:
8.2 Why Training Error Is Not Enough
A model is useful only if it generalizes. Training error measures how well the fitted model describes data it has already seen. Because the model was chosen to fit those observations, training error is usually optimistic. The more flexible the model, the easier it is to drive training error down without improving future predictions.
The validation-set approach addresses this optimism by splitting the data into a training set and a held-out validation or test set. The model is fit only on the training set, and prediction error is computed on observations not used during fitting.

RPython



library(ISLR)
library(boot)
library(ggplot2)

auto <- na.omit(ISLR::Auto)

set.seed(571)
train_id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(auto)), size = 0.6 * nrow(auto))
train <- auto[train_id, ]
test <- auto[-train_id, ]

fit <- lm(mpg ~ horsepower, data = train)
pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
mean((test$mpg - pred)^2)




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
auto = pd.DataFrame({
    "horsepower": rng.uniform(45, 230, 392)
})
auto["mpg"] = (
    48 - 0.18 * auto["horsepower"] +
    0.00035 * auto["horsepower"] ** 2 +
    rng.normal(0, 3, len(auto))
)

train, test = train_test_split(auto, train_size=0.6, random_state=571)
fit = smf.ols("mpg ~ horsepower", data=train).fit()
pred = fit.predict(test)
print(mean_squared_error(test["mpg"], pred))




The validation-set estimate is easy to understand, but it depends on which observations happen to fall in the training set. If we change the random split, the estimated test error can change as well.

title: 8  Model Assessment and Resampling
section: 8.3 Polynomial Complexity in the Auto Data
text:
8.3 Polynomial Complexity in the Auto Data
The Auto data show a curved relationship between horsepower and gas mileage. A straight line is too rigid, but an extremely high-degree polynomial may fit noise. Resampling gives a disciplined way to compare model flexibility.

RPython



ggplot(auto, aes(horsepower, mpg)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ poly(x, 2),
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#2f5f7e"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ poly(x, 4),
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#7a3035"
  )




import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.regplot(data=auto, x="horsepower", y="mpg", order=1, scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.65})
sns.regplot(data=auto, x="horsepower", y="mpg", order=2, scatter=False, color="#2f5f7e")
sns.regplot(data=auto, x="horsepower", y="mpg", order=4, scatter=False, color="#7a3035")
plt.show()




For one split, compute validation error for polynomial degrees 1 through 10:

RPython



set.seed(571)
train_id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(auto)), size = 0.6 * nrow(auto))
train <- auto[train_id, ]
test <- auto[-train_id, ]

validation_error <- sapply(1:10, function(degree) {
  fit <- lm(mpg ~ poly(horsepower, degree), data = train)
  pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
  mean((test$mpg - pred)^2)
})

data.frame(degree = 1:10, mse = validation_error)




from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

validation_error = []

for degree in range(1, 11):
    model = make_pipeline(
        PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False),
        LinearRegression()
    )
    model.fit(train[["horsepower"]], train["mpg"])
    pred = model.predict(test[["horsepower"]])
    validation_error.append(mean_squared_error(test["mpg"], pred))

print(pd.DataFrame({"degree": range(1, 11), "mse": validation_error}))




The usual pattern is a sharp improvement from degree 1 to degree 2 and little consistent gain from higher degrees. The important lesson is not the exact best degree for one split; it is that the answer can vary when the split changes.

RPython



split_errors <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:10, function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  train_id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(auto)), size = 0.6 * nrow(auto))
  train <- auto[train_id, ]
  test <- auto[-train_id, ]

  data.frame(
    split = seed,
    degree = 1:10,
    mse = sapply(1:10, function(degree) {
      fit <- lm(mpg ~ poly(horsepower, degree), data = train)
      pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
      mean((test$mpg - pred)^2)
    })
  )
}))

ggplot(split_errors, aes(degree, mse, group = split)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45)




split_records = []

for seed in range(1, 11):
    train_i, test_i = train_test_split(auto, train_size=0.6, random_state=seed)
    for degree in range(1, 11):
        model = make_pipeline(
            PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False),
            LinearRegression()
        )
        model.fit(train_i[["horsepower"]], train_i["mpg"])
        pred = model.predict(test_i[["horsepower"]])
        split_records.append({
            "split": seed,
            "degree": degree,
            "mse": mean_squared_error(test_i["mpg"], pred)
        })

split_errors = pd.DataFrame(split_records)
sns.lineplot(data=split_errors, x="degree", y="mse", units="split", estimator=None, alpha=0.45)
plt.show()




Repeated splits usually agree that a quadratic model is much better than a line, but they need not agree on every detail. This instability motivates cross-validation.

title: 8  Model Assessment and Resampling
text:
8.4 Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation
Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) uses each observation once as a validation point. For observation i, fit the model on all observations except i, predict the held-out response, and compute

MSE_i = (y_i - \hat y_i)^2.

The LOOCV estimate averages these n errors:

CV_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} MSE_i.

The boot::cv.glm() function performs LOOCV when K is omitted. A linear model can be fit with glm() using its default Gaussian family.

RPython



loocv_error <- function(degree) {
  fit <- glm(mpg ~ poly(horsepower, degree), data = auto)
  cv.glm(auto, fit)$delta[1]
}

sapply(1:5, loocv_error)




from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut, cross_val_score

def loocv_error(degree):
    model = make_pipeline(
        PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False),
        LinearRegression()
    )
    scores = cross_val_score(
        model,
        auto[["horsepower"]],
        auto["mpg"],
        cv=LeaveOneOut(),
        scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
    )
    return -scores.mean()

print([loocv_error(degree) for degree in range(1, 6)])




LOOCV uses nearly all observations for every fit, so it tends to have low bias as an estimate of test error. Its disadvantage is computation: large data sets or slow models can make LOOCV expensive.

title: 8  Model Assessment and Resampling
text:
8.5 k-Fold Cross-Validation
k-fold cross-validation divides the data into k roughly equal folds. For each fold, fit the model on the other k - 1 folds and evaluate on the held-out fold. The estimate is

CV_{(k)} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k} MSE_j.

LOOCV is the special case where k=n. In applied work, k=5 or k=10 is often a good compromise between statistical stability and computational cost.

RPython



kfold_error <- function(degree, k = 10) {
  fit <- glm(mpg ~ poly(horsepower, degree), data = auto)
  cv.glm(auto, fit, K = k)$delta[1]
}

data.frame(
  degree = 1:5,
  loocv = sapply(1:5, loocv_error),
  ten_fold = sapply(1:5, kfold_error)
)




from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

def kfold_error(degree, k=10):
    model = make_pipeline(
        PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False),
        LinearRegression()
    )
    scores = cross_val_score(
        model,
        auto[["horsepower"]],
        auto["mpg"],
        cv=KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=571),
        scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
    )
    return -scores.mean()

print(pd.DataFrame({
    "degree": range(1, 6),
    "loocv": [loocv_error(degree) for degree in range(1, 6)],
    "ten_fold": [kfold_error(degree) for degree in range(1, 6)]
}))




The LOOCV and 10-fold estimates should tell the same broad story: quadratic curvature matters, while higher-degree terms should be justified by their estimated out-of-sample performance rather than by training fit alone.

title: 8  Model Assessment and Resampling
text:
8.6 Comparing Candidate Sales Models
The same logic applies to ordinary regression workflows. The Carseats data contain simulated sales of child car seats at 400 stores. Suppose we want to compare a full model with all predictors against a reduced model that focuses on predictors with a clearer sales mechanism.

RPython



carseats <- ISLR::Carseats

set.seed(571)
train_id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(carseats)), size = 0.8 * nrow(carseats))
train <- carseats[train_id, ]
test <- carseats[-train_id, ]

full_fit <- lm(Sales ~ ., data = train)
reduced_fit <- lm(
  Sales ~ CompPrice + Income + Advertising + Price + ShelveLoc + Age,
  data = train
)




rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
carseats = pd.DataFrame({
    "Sales": rng.normal(8, 2, 400),
    "CompPrice": rng.normal(125, 15, 400),
    "Income": rng.normal(70, 25, 400),
    "Advertising": rng.uniform(0, 25, 400),
    "Price": rng.normal(115, 20, 400),
    "ShelveLoc": rng.choice(["Bad", "Medium", "Good"], 400),
    "Age": rng.normal(55, 15, 400),
    "Population": rng.normal(250, 100, 400)
})

train, test = train_test_split(carseats, train_size=0.8, random_state=571)
full_fit = smf.ols(
    "Sales ~ CompPrice + Income + Advertising + Price + C(ShelveLoc) + Age + Population",
    data=train
).fit()
reduced_fit = smf.ols(
    "Sales ~ CompPrice + Income + Advertising + Price + C(ShelveLoc) + Age",
    data=train
).fit()




Residual standard error describes in-sample residual size. Test-set RMSE and test-set R^2 describe predictive performance on held-out observations.

RPython



model_metrics <- function(fit, test_data, model_name) {
  pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test_data)
  actual <- test_data$Sales

  rmse <- sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))
  test_r2 <- 1 - sum((actual - pred)^2) /
    sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)

  data.frame(
    model = model_name,
    residual_se = sigma(fit),
    rmse = rmse,
    test_r2 = test_r2
  )
}

rbind(
  model_metrics(full_fit, test, "Full model"),
  model_metrics(reduced_fit, test, "Reduced model")
)




def model_metrics(fit, test_data, model_name):
    pred = fit.predict(test_data)
    actual = test_data["Sales"]
    rmse = mean_squared_error(actual, pred) ** 0.5
    test_r2 = 1 - ((actual - pred) ** 2).sum() / ((actual - actual.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    return {
        "model": model_name,
        "residual_se": np.sqrt(fit.scale),
        "rmse": rmse,
        "test_r2": test_r2
    }

print(pd.DataFrame([
    model_metrics(full_fit, test, "Full model"),
    model_metrics(reduced_fit, test, "Reduced model")
]))




Because the reduced model is nested inside the full model, an ANOVA comparison can ask whether the omitted predictors improve the fit after the reduced model’s predictors are already included.

RPython



anova(reduced_fit, full_fit)




from statsmodels.stats.anova import anova_lm

print(anova_lm(reduced_fit, full_fit))




Model comparison should combine statistical evidence, test performance, and interpretability. A slightly larger model is not automatically better if its added variables do not improve generalization or clarify the substantive claim.
Cross-validation lets us compare the same two models without relying on one train/test split:

RPython



glm_full <- glm(Sales ~ ., data = carseats)
glm_reduced <- glm(
  Sales ~ CompPrice + Income + Advertising + Price + ShelveLoc + Age,
  data = carseats
)

data.frame(
  model = c("Full model", "Reduced model"),
  cv_5 = c(
    cv.glm(carseats, glm_full, K = 5)$delta[1],
    cv.glm(carseats, glm_reduced, K = 5)$delta[1]
  ),
  cv_10 = c(
    cv.glm(carseats, glm_full, K = 10)$delta[1],
    cv.glm(carseats, glm_reduced, K = 10)$delta[1]
  ),
  loocv = c(
    cv.glm(carseats, glm_full)$delta[1],
    cv.glm(carseats, glm_reduced)$delta[1]
  )
)




from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X_full = carseats.drop(columns=["Sales"])
y_sales = carseats["Sales"]
X_reduced = carseats[["CompPrice", "Income", "Advertising", "Price", "ShelveLoc", "Age"]]

def cv_rmse(X, y, k):
    categorical = X.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns
    preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
        ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical)
    ], remainder="passthrough")
    model = make_pipeline(preprocess, LinearRegression())
    scores = cross_val_score(
        model, X, y,
        cv=KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=571),
        scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
    )
    return (-scores.mean()) ** 0.5

print(pd.DataFrame({
    "model": ["Full model", "Reduced model"],
    "cv_5": [cv_rmse(X_full, y_sales, 5), cv_rmse(X_reduced, y_sales, 5)],
    "cv_10": [cv_rmse(X_full, y_sales, 10), cv_rmse(X_reduced, y_sales, 10)]
}))

text:
8.7 Simulated Nonlinear Data
A simulation makes the role of model complexity visible because we know the data were generated from a nonlinear pattern.

RPython



set.seed(571)
sim <- data.frame(x = runif(100, min = -10, max = 10))
sim$y <- sin(sim$x) + 0.1 * sim$x^2 + rnorm(100)

plot(y ~ x, data = sim, pch = 19, col = "#2f5f7e")




rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
sim = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.uniform(-10, 10, 100)})
sim["y"] = np.sin(sim["x"]) + 0.1 * sim["x"] ** 2 + rng.normal(size=100)

plt.scatter(sim["x"], sim["y"], color="#2f5f7e")
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("y")
plt.show()




Fit polynomial models and use 10-fold cross-validation to estimate generalization error:

RPython



poly_cv <- sapply(1:15, function(degree) {
  fit <- glm(y ~ poly(x, degree), data = sim)
  cv.glm(sim, fit, K = 10)$delta[1]
})

plot(
  1:15,
  poly_cv,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "Polynomial degree",
  ylab = "10-fold CV error"
)




poly_cv = [
    -cross_val_score(
        make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False), LinearRegression()),
        sim[["x"]],
        sim["y"],
        cv=KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=571),
        scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
    ).mean()
    for degree in range(1, 16)
]

plt.plot(range(1, 16), poly_cv, marker="o")
plt.xlabel("Polynomial degree")
plt.ylabel("10-fold CV error")
plt.show()




This exercise separates visual fit from estimated generalization. A model with many degrees may trace the observed points closely, but cross-validation asks whether that flexibility is likely to help on new data.

title: 8  Model Assessment and Resampling
text:
8.8 Bootstrapping
Cross-validation estimates prediction error. Bootstrapping estimates uncertainty. A bootstrap sample draws n rows from the original data, with replacement, and recomputes a statistic on the sampled data. After many bootstrap samples, the spread of the bootstrap estimates describes the statistic’s sampling variability.
If \hat\alpha^{*1}, \ldots, \hat\alpha^{*B} are bootstrap estimates, the bootstrap standard error is

SE_B(\hat\alpha)
= \sqrt{
\frac{1}{B-1}
\sum_{r=1}^{B}
\left(
\hat\alpha^{*r}
- \frac{1}{B}\sum_{s=1}^{B}\hat\alpha^{*s}
\right)^2
}.

For the Portfolio data, one statistic of interest is the allocation that minimizes variance across two assets:

\hat\alpha =
\frac{\hat\sigma_Y^2 - \hat\sigma_{XY}}
{\hat\sigma_X^2 + \hat\sigma_Y^2 - 2\hat\sigma_{XY}}.


RPython



portfolio <- ISLR::Portfolio

alpha_stat <- function(data, index) {
  x <- data$X[index]
  y <- data$Y[index]
  (var(y) - cov(x, y)) / (var(x) + var(y) - 2 * cov(x, y))
}

set.seed(571)
boot(portfolio, alpha_stat, R = 1000)




rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
portfolio = pd.DataFrame({
    "X": rng.normal(0, 1, 100),
    "Y": rng.normal(0, 1, 100)
})

def alpha_stat(data):
    x = data["X"]
    y = data["Y"]
    return (y.var() - x.cov(y)) / (x.var() + y.var() - 2 * x.cov(y))

boot_alpha = []
for _ in range(1000):
    sample = portfolio.sample(len(portfolio), replace=True, random_state=rng.integers(1_000_000))
    boot_alpha.append(alpha_stat(sample))

print(pd.Series(boot_alpha).describe())




The same idea applies to regression coefficients. The function below refits the model on each bootstrap sample and returns the intercept and slope.

RPython



boot_lm <- function(data, index) {
  coef(lm(mpg ~ horsepower, data = data, subset = index))
}

set.seed(571)
boot(auto, boot_lm, R = 1000)




boot_lm = []
for _ in range(1000):
    sample = auto.sample(len(auto), replace=True, random_state=rng.integers(1_000_000))
    fit = smf.ols("mpg ~ horsepower", data=sample).fit()
    boot_lm.append(fit.params)

print(pd.DataFrame(boot_lm).describe())




If a nonlinear mean structure is more appropriate, bootstrap the quadratic model instead:

RPython



boot_quad <- function(data, index) {
  coef(lm(mpg ~ poly(horsepower, 2), data = data, subset = index))
}

set.seed(571)
boot(auto, boot_quad, R = 1000)




boot_quad = []
for _ in range(1000):
    sample = auto.sample(len(auto), replace=True, random_state=rng.integers(1_000_000))
    sample = sample.assign(horsepower2=sample["horsepower"] ** 2)
    fit = smf.ols("mpg ~ horsepower + horsepower2", data=sample).fit()
    boot_quad.append(fit.params)

print(pd.DataFrame(boot_quad).describe())




The bootstrap does not replace model criticism. It quantifies variability for the statistic implied by the model and the data collection process. If the model is misspecified or the data are not representative, the bootstrap can still give a precise answer to the wrong question.

9.2 Splitting Comes First
A split creates a contract. The training data are used to estimate preprocessing steps, fit models, and tune candidate choices. The test data are held back for final evaluation.

RPython



library(rsample)
library(AmesHousing)
library(modeldata)

# To get the processed version:
ames <- make_ames()

set.seed(571)
ames_split <- initial_split(ames, prop = 0.8, strata = Sale_Price)
ames_train <- training(ames_split)
ames_test <- testing(ames_split)




from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

ames_train, ames_test = train_test_split(
    ames,
    train_size=0.8,
    random_state=571
)




Stratification keeps the response distribution roughly comparable across partitions. This is useful when the response is skewed or when a class outcome is imbalanced.

title: 9  Data Splitting and Feature Engineering
text:
9.3 Leakage
Leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time enters the model-building process. Common examples include:







Step
Leakage risk




Scaling before splitting
Test-set means and standard deviations influence training data


Imputing before splitting
Test-set missingness affects imputation values


Selecting predictors before splitting
Test-set associations influence the model space


Tuning on the test set
Final evaluation becomes part of model selection


Using future variables
Predictors contain information not known at decision time



The anti-leakage rule is simple: learn preprocessing from the training data, then apply the learned transformation to validation, test, and future data.

title: 9  Data Splitting and Feature Engineering
text:
9.4 Ames Housing Workflow
For Ames housing, Sale_Price is the target and many predictors are categorical, skewed, sparse, or missing. A reproducible feature workflow should handle all of these in a fixed order.

RPython



library(recipes)

ames_recipe <-
  recipe(Sale_Price ~ ., data = ames_train) |>
  step_log(Sale_Price, base = 10, skip = TRUE) |>
  step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.01) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

ames_prep <- prep(ames_recipe, training = ames_train)
train_ready <- bake(ames_prep, new_data = NULL)
test_ready <- bake(ames_prep, new_data = ames_test)




import numpy as np
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

y_train = np.log10(ames_train["Sale_Price"])
X_train = ames_train.drop(columns=["Sale_Price"])
X_test = ames_test.drop(columns=["Sale_Price"])

numeric_features = X_train.select_dtypes(include="number").columns
categorical_features = X_train.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns

numeric_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler())
])
categorical_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("dummy", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))
])

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("numeric", numeric_pipeline, numeric_features),
    ("categorical", categorical_pipeline, categorical_features)
])

train_ready = preprocess.fit_transform(X_train)
test_ready = preprocess.transform(X_test)




The recipe is estimated on ames_train. The test data receive the same learned mapping: the same rare-level rules, dummy columns, zero-variance filter, and normalization constants.

9.5 Transformations
Transformations change the representation of predictors or the response. They can make simple models more effective, but they also change interpretation.








Transformation
When useful

Standardization

title: 9  Data Splitting and Feature Engineering
text:
9.6 Interaction Features
An interaction is feature construction with a statistical interpretation. In the model

\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X,Z)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1X + \beta_2Z + \beta_3XZ,

the effect of X changes with Z. Interactions are especially useful when theory or visualization suggests that a relationship differs by group or by level of another variable.
In housing data, the effect of living area might differ by neighborhood or overall quality. In advertising data, the return to TV spending might depend on radio spending. Interactions should be evaluated with held-out error and interpreted with marginal effects or predicted values, not only with coefficient signs.
crumbs: 9  Data Splitting and Feature Engineering

title: 9  Data Splitting and Feature Engineering
text:
9.7 Model-Ready Data Is Not Model-Free
Preprocessing embeds modeling choices. Scaling assumes that relative distance matters. Rare-level lumping assumes sparse categories should share information. Dummy encoding chooses a reference structure. Feature engineering is therefore part of the model, and it must be reported with the same care as the final algorithm.

title: 10  Model Selection and Regularization
text:
10.1 Learning Objectives
Model selection asks which predictors and which level of complexity should be used. Regularization answers the same question by changing the estimation problem: instead of choosing one subset of predictors directly, it penalizes coefficient size or coefficient count.

title: 10  Model Selection and Regularization
text:
Compare best subset, forward stepwise, and backward stepwise selection.
Use adjusted R^2, C_p, BIC, AIC, validation error, and cross-validation error.
Explain ridge regression and lasso as penalized least squares.
Describe why standardization matters for penalized regression.
Use cross-validation to choose a tuning parameter.

title: 10  Model Selection and Regularization
text:
10.2 Why Selection Is Hard
With p predictors, best subset selection considers 2^p possible models. That search can find a model that fits the training data well, but the search itself adds variability. The selected model may look more certain than it really is because the same data were used to try many alternatives.
Selection should therefore be evaluated with a criterion that accounts for complexity or with held-out prediction error.

title: 10  Model Selection and Regularization
text:
10.3 Subset and Stepwise Selection
Best subset selection chooses the best model of each size. Forward stepwise selection starts from the intercept-only model and adds one predictor at a time. Backward stepwise selection starts from the full model and removes one predictor at a time.

RPython



library(leaps)

subset_fit <- regsubsets(Sale_Price ~ ., data = train, nvmax = 20)
subset_summary <- summary(subset_fit)

which.min(subset_summary$bic)
which.max(subset_summary$adjr2)




import itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

predictors = [col for col in train.columns if col != "Sale_Price"]
records = []

for size in range(1, min(len(predictors), 5) + 1):
    for cols in itertools.combinations(predictors, size):
        X = sm.add_constant(pd.get_dummies(train[list(cols)], drop_first=True))
        fit = sm.OLS(train["Sale_Price"], X).fit()
        records.append({
            "size": size,
            "predictors": cols,
            "aic": fit.aic,
            "bic": fit.bic,
            "adj_r2": fit.rsquared_adj
        })

subset_summary = pd.DataFrame(records)
print(subset_summary.sort_values("bic").head())
print(subset_summary.sort_values("adj_r2", ascending=False).head())




The resulting model path can be compared using:








Criterion
Preference
Caution




Training RSS
Larger models
Always decreases as predictors are added


Adjusted R^2
Fit adjusted for model size
Still an in-sample measure


Mallows’ C_p
Low estimated prediction error
Depends on variance estimate


AIC
Predictive fit with lighter penalty
Can select larger models


BIC
Fit with stronger penalty
Often selects simpler models


Cross-validation
Held-out predictive performance
Depends on split design

title: 10  Model Selection and Regularization
text:
10.4 Media Incivility Selection Example
A model-selection analysis should connect the criterion to the research question. For a media-incivility outcome with many political, platform, or text features, an exhaustive search can identify candidate models of each size, while forward and backward selection provide computationally cheaper alternatives.
The analysis workflow is:

define the outcome and candidate predictors,
split the data or define cross-validation folds,
fit the candidate model paths on the training data,
compare R^2, adjusted R^2, C_p, BIC, and validation error,
refit the selected specification on the training data,
evaluate once on the held-out data,
describe the selected predictors without overstating certainty.

title: 10  Model Selection and Regularization
text:
10.5 Ridge Regression
Ridge regression minimizes

\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2
+ \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2.

The \ell_2 penalty shrinks coefficients toward zero but usually does not set them exactly to zero. Ridge is especially helpful when predictors are correlated: it distributes signal across related variables and lowers variance.

RPython



library(glmnet)

x_train <- model.matrix(Apps ~ ., College)[, -1]
y_train <- College$Apps

ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0)
coef(ridge_cv, s = "lambda.min")
coef(ridge_cv, s = "lambda.1se")




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

x_train = pd.get_dummies(college.drop(columns=["Apps"]), drop_first=True)
y_train = college["Apps"]

ridge_cv = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 100))
)
ridge_cv.fit(x_train, y_train)

print(ridge_cv.named_steps["ridgecv"].alpha_)

title: 10  Model Selection and Regularization
text:
10.6 Lasso
The lasso minimizes

\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2
+ \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|.

The \ell_1 penalty can set coefficients exactly to zero, so lasso is both a prediction method and a variable-selection method. When predictors are strongly correlated, lasso may choose one representative predictor and ignore others with similar information.

RPython



lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1)
coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.min")
coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.1se")




from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

lasso_cv = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LassoCV(cv=10, random_state=571, max_iter=10000)
)
lasso_cv.fit(x_train, y_train)

print(lasso_cv.named_steps["lassocv"].alpha_)




lambda.min gives the value with the lowest cross-validation error. lambda.1se gives the simplest model whose error is within one standard error of the minimum. The one-standard-error rule is often a good teaching device because it makes the accuracy-simplicity tradeoff explicit.

title: 10  Model Selection and Regularization
text:
10.7 Scaling and Interpretation
Penalties operate on coefficient size, so predictors must be on comparable scales. Otherwise a variable measured in large units may be penalized differently from a variable measured in small units. Most software standardizes predictors internally by default, but analysts should know whether and how that standardization occurred.
After penalized regression, coefficient interpretation should be careful. Shrinkage intentionally biases coefficients toward zero to reduce variance. Penalized coefficients are not ordinary least-squares estimates with ordinary standard errors.

title: 11  Dimension Reduction
text:
11.1 Learning Objectives
Dimension reduction replaces many correlated variables with a smaller set of constructed features. The goal may be visualization, compression, noise reduction, or prediction when the original predictor space is too large or too collinear for stable ordinary regression.

title: 11  Dimension Reduction
text:
Explain principal components as directions of maximal variance.
Distinguish PCA, principal components regression, and partial least squares.
Explain why centering and scaling change principal components.
Use cross-validation to choose the number of components.
Interpret component loadings and prediction results together.

title: 11  Dimension Reduction
text:
11.2 Principal Components
Let X be a centered and scaled predictor matrix. Principal component analysis finds loading vectors v_1, v_2,\ldots so that

z_1 = Xv_1

has the largest possible variance subject to \|v_1\|=1. The second component maximizes variance subject to being orthogonal to the first, and so on. The score vectors z_1,z_2,\ldots are new predictors: uncorrelated linear combinations of the original variables.
PCA is unsupervised. It uses only X, not the response Y.

title: 11  Dimension Reduction
text:
11.3 Scaling Is a Modeling Choice
PCA is sensitive to measurement units. If one predictor has values in thousands and another has values in fractions, the first can dominate the components even if it is not more important. Centering removes location differences; scaling puts variables on comparable units.

RPython



college <- ISLR::College
x <- model.matrix(Apps ~ ., college)[, -1]

pca_unscaled <- prcomp(x, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
pca_scaled <- prcomp(x, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

summary(pca_scaled)
biplot(pca_scaled, scale = 0)




import pandas as pd
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

x = pd.get_dummies(college.drop(columns=["Apps"]), drop_first=True)

pca_unscaled = PCA().fit(x)
x_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(x)
pca_scaled = PCA().fit(x_scaled)

print(pca_scaled.explained_variance_ratio_[:5])




An incorrect workflow scales the full data set before splitting, which leaks information. A correct workflow estimates centering, scaling, and components from the training data, then applies the learned rotation to held-out data.

title: 11  Dimension Reduction
text:
11.4 Principal Components Regression
Principal components regression first constructs components from the predictors, then regresses the outcome on the first M components.

RPython



library(pls)

set.seed(571)
pcr_fit <- pcr(
  Apps ~ .,
  data = college,
  scale = TRUE,
  validation = "CV"
)

validationplot(pcr_fit, val.type = "MSEP")




import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

component_grid = range(1, 11)
pcr_scores = []

for n_components in component_grid:
    pcr = make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        PCA(n_components=n_components),
        LinearRegression()
    )
    mse = -cross_val_score(
        pcr, x, college["Apps"],
        scoring="neg_mean_squared_error",
        cv=10
    ).mean()
    pcr_scores.append(mse)

print(list(zip(component_grid, pcr_scores)))




Keeping too few components can miss predictive signal. Keeping too many components can reintroduce noise. Cross-validation provides an empirical way to choose M.

title: 11  Dimension Reduction
text:
11.5 Partial Least Squares
Partial least squares also constructs components, but it uses the response while constructing them. This can help when directions with large predictor variance are not the directions most related to the outcome.

RPython



pls_fit <- plsr(
  Apps ~ .,
  data = college,
  scale = TRUE,
  validation = "CV"
)

validationplot(pls_fit, val.type = "MSEP")




from sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

pls_scores = []

for n_components in component_grid:
    pls = make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        PLSRegression(n_components=n_components)
    )
    mse = -cross_val_score(
        pls, x, college["Apps"],
        scoring="neg_mean_squared_error",
        cv=10
    ).mean()
    pls_scores.append(mse)

print(list(zip(component_grid, pls_scores)))







Method
Uses Y to construct components?
Main purpose




PCA
No
Exploration and compression


PCR
No, then regression
Prediction with correlated predictors


PLS
Yes
Prediction when response-related directions matter

title: 11  Dimension Reduction
text:
11.6 Near-Infrared Spectra Example
High-dimensional spectra data illustrate why dimension reduction is useful. Each observation can contain hundreds of wavelength measurements, with neighboring wavelengths strongly correlated. A small number of components can summarize broad spectral patterns while reducing noise.
The analysis sequence is:

center and scale spectral predictors inside the training data,
visualize the first two component scores,
inspect loadings to see which wavelengths define each component,
fit PCR and PLS models,
choose the number of components by cross-validation,
evaluate the selected model on held-out observations.

This example also shows that interpretability changes. Instead of interpreting one coefficient per wavelength, students interpret component loadings and prediction performance together.

12.1 Learning Objectives
This chapter connects model flexibility to prediction error and then uses nonlinear regression tools to show how simple models can learn curved relationships without abandoning statistical interpretation.

title: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models
text:
12.2 Bias-Variance Decomposition
At a new point x_0, expected prediction error can be decomposed as

\operatorname{E}\{(Y - \hat f(x_0))^2\}
= \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)
+ \operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0))^2
+ \operatorname{Var}(\hat f(x_0)).

The irreducible error \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon) remains even if the true regression function is known. Bias is error from using a model that is too rigid. Variance is error from using a model that changes too much across training samples.
Increasing flexibility usually lowers bias and raises variance. The best predictive model is the one that balances these forces for the available sample size and signal strength.
crumbs: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models

title: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models
text:
12.3 Simulation View
A simulation makes the tradeoff visible because the true function can be known:

RPython



set.seed(571)
x <- runif(200, -3, 3)
y <- sin(x) + 0.4 * x^2 + rnorm(200, sd = 0.4)

fit_linear <- lm(y ~ x)
fit_poly5 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 5))
fit_poly15 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 15))




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 200)
y = np.sin(x) + 0.4 * x**2 + rng.normal(0, 0.4, 200)
X = x.reshape(-1, 1)

fit_linear = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
fit_poly5 = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(5), LinearRegression()).fit(X, y)
fit_poly15 = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(15), LinearRegression()).fit(X, y)




The linear model has high bias if the true function is curved. The degree-15 polynomial may have high variance if it follows accidental noise. Validation error, not visual smoothness alone, should guide the choice.
crumbs: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models

title: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models
text:
12.4 Polynomial Regression
Polynomial regression remains linear in the coefficients while allowing a curved mean function:

\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X=x)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2x^2 + \cdots + \beta_dx^d.

In R, orthogonal polynomial terms reduce numerical collinearity:

RPython



library(ISLR)

wage <- ISLR::Wage
poly_fit <- lm(wage ~ poly(age, 4), data = wage)




from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

X_age = wage[["age"]]
y_wage = wage["wage"]

poly_fit = make_pipeline(
    PolynomialFeatures(degree=4, include_bias=False),
    LinearRegression()
).fit(X_age, y_wage)




The degree controls flexibility. Prediction plots are usually clearer than raw coefficient interpretation for high-degree polynomials.
crumbs: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models

title: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models
text:
12.5 Step Functions and Splines
A step function divides a predictor into intervals and fits a constant mean within each interval:

RPython



step_fit <- lm(wage ~ cut(age, 4), data = wage)




import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

wage_step = wage.copy()
wage_step["age_bin"] = pd.cut(wage_step["age"], bins=4)
step_fit = smf.ols("wage ~ C(age_bin)", data=wage_step).fit()
print(step_fit.summary())




Regression splines fit smooth piecewise polynomials. Knots define where the pieces meet, and degrees of freedom control smoothness:

RPython



library(splines)

spline_fit <- lm(wage ~ bs(age, df = 6), data = wage)
natural_fit <- lm(wage ~ ns(age, df = 5), data = wage)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

spline_fit = smf.ols(
    "wage ~ bs(age, df=6)",
    data=wage
).fit()
natural_fit = smf.ols(
    "wage ~ cr(age, df=5)",
    data=wage
).fit()




Natural splines add boundary constraints that often produce more stable behavior at the edges of the data.
crumbs: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models

title: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models
text:
12.6 Generalized Additive Models
Generalized additive models combine several smooth functions:

g\{\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X)\}
= \beta_0 + f_1(X_1) + f_2(X_2) + \cdots + f_p(X_p).

They keep additivity while allowing nonlinear effects:

RPython



library(gam)

gam_fit <- gam(
  wage ~ s(age, df = 5) + s(year, df = 4) + education,
  data = wage
)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

gam_like_fit = smf.ols(
    "wage ~ bs(age, df=5) + bs(year, df=4) + C(education)",
    data=wage
).fit()




GAM plots show the estimated contribution of each smooth term while holding other terms in the model fixed.
crumbs: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models

title: 12  Bias, Variance, and Nonlinear Models
text:
12.7 Choosing Flexibility
Training error usually decreases as flexibility increases. Test error often decreases at first, then increases when the model starts fitting noise. A reliable comparison should use a validation set or cross-validation:

choose a grid of degrees, knots, or smoothness values,
fit each candidate using the training folds,
compute held-out error,
choose a flexible model only if it earns better generalization,
explain the fitted shape with prediction plots.

title: 13  Polynomial Regression and Step Functions
text:
13.2 Polynomial Terms
A degree-d polynomial regression has the form

\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X=x)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2x^2 + \cdots + \beta_dx^d.

The model is linear in the coefficients even though it is nonlinear in x.

RPython



set.seed(571)
n <- 250
nonlinear <- data.frame(age = runif(n, 18, 70))
nonlinear$wage <- 18 + 2.1 * nonlinear$age -
  0.025 * nonlinear$age^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 8)

poly2 <- lm(wage ~ poly(age, 2), data = nonlinear)
poly4 <- lm(wage ~ poly(age, 4), data = nonlinear)
summary(poly2)




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
n = 250
nonlinear = pd.DataFrame({"age": rng.uniform(18, 70, n)})
nonlinear["wage"] = (
    18 + 2.1 * nonlinear["age"] -
    0.025 * nonlinear["age"] ** 2 +
    rng.normal(0, 8, n)
)

poly2 = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(2, include_bias=False), LinearRegression())
poly4 = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(4, include_bias=False), LinearRegression())
poly2.fit(nonlinear[["age"]], nonlinear["wage"])
poly4.fit(nonlinear[["age"]], nonlinear["wage"])




High-degree polynomials can behave poorly near the boundaries of the data. Validation should decide whether additional degree earns better generalization.
crumbs: 13  Polynomial Regression and Step Functions

title: 13  Polynomial Regression and Step Functions
text:
13.3 Step Functions
A step function turns a continuous predictor into intervals:

\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1I(X \in C_1) + \cdots + \beta_KI(X \in C_K).


RPython



step_fit <- lm(wage ~ cut(age, breaks = 5), data = nonlinear)
summary(step_fit)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

step_data = nonlinear.copy()
step_data["age_bin"] = pd.cut(step_data["age"], bins=5)
step_fit = smf.ols("wage ~ C(age_bin)", data=step_data).fit()
print(step_fit.summary())




Step functions are easy to explain but can create artificial jumps at cut points. They are useful when thresholds are substantively meaningful or when interpretability matters more than smoothness.

14.1 Learning Objectives
Splines and generalized additive models provide flexible nonlinear regression without forcing one global polynomial to describe the entire relationship. They are especially useful when the fitted curve should be smooth but locally adaptive.

title: 14  Splines and Generalized Additive Models
text:
14.2 Regression Splines
A regression spline fits piecewise polynomials that join at knots. The number and placement of knots control flexibility.

RPython



library(splines)

set.seed(571)
n <- 250
spline_data <- data.frame(age = runif(n, 18, 70))
spline_data$wage <- 20 + 1.8 * spline_data$age -
  0.02 * spline_data$age^2 + sin(spline_data$age / 5) * 4 +
  rnorm(n, sd = 7)

spline_fit <- lm(wage ~ bs(age, df = 6), data = spline_data)
natural_fit <- lm(wage ~ ns(age, df = 5), data = spline_data)
summary(spline_fit)




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
n = 250
spline_data = pd.DataFrame({"age": rng.uniform(18, 70, n)})
spline_data["wage"] = (
    20 + 1.8 * spline_data["age"] -
    0.02 * spline_data["age"] ** 2 +
    np.sin(spline_data["age"] / 5) * 4 +
    rng.normal(0, 7, n)
)

spline_fit = smf.ols("wage ~ bs(age, df=6)", data=spline_data).fit()
natural_fit = smf.ols("wage ~ cr(age, df=5)", data=spline_data).fit()
print(spline_fit.summary())




Natural splines add boundary constraints, which often stabilize fitted curves near the smallest and largest observed values.

title: 14  Splines and Generalized Additive Models
text:
14.3 Generalized Additive Models
A generalized additive model has the form

g\{\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X)\}
= \beta_0 + f_1(X_1) + f_2(X_2) + \cdots + f_p(X_p).

The model is additive across predictors but nonlinear within each predictor.

RPython



library(gam)

gam_fit <- gam(wage ~ s(age, df = 5), data = spline_data)
summary(gam_fit)




gam_like_fit = smf.ols("wage ~ bs(age, df=5)", data=spline_data).fit()
print(gam_like_fit.summary())




The fitted smooth term should be interpreted with predicted values and uncertainty, not as a single slope.

title: 15  Classification Model Comparison
text:
15.1 Learning Objectives
Classification model comparison asks which probability model is most useful for the decision at hand. Logistic regression, LDA, and QDA can all return class probabilities, but they make different assumptions and can behave differently under imbalance, nonlinear boundaries, and threshold changes.

title: 15  Classification Model Comparison
text:
Compare logistic regression, LDA, and QDA on the same task.
Distinguish probability quality from hard-label accuracy.
Explain how thresholds change sensitivity and specificity.
Use ROC curves, AUC, and calibration to compare classifiers.
Choose a classifier based on the decision context rather than one metric alone.

title: 15  Classification Model Comparison
text:
15.2 Logistic Regression Baseline
For a binary outcome, logistic regression models

p(x) = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid X=x).

The logit link maps probabilities to the real line:

\log\left(\frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}\right)
= \beta_0 + x^\top\beta.

Equivalently,

p(x) =
\frac{\exp(\beta_0 + x^\top\beta)}
{1 + \exp(\beta_0 + x^\top\beta)}.

Coefficients are changes in log odds. Exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio, holding the other predictors fixed.

title: 15  Classification Model Comparison
text:
15.3 Credit Default Example
The default data show why probability estimation matters. The response is rare, so accuracy can be misleading: a classifier that predicts “no default” for everyone may have high accuracy but no practical value.

RPython



library(ISLR)

default_fit <- glm(
  default ~ student + balance + income,
  data = Default,
  family = binomial
)

summary(default_fit)
exp(coef(default_fit))
Default$prob_default <- predict(default_fit, type = "response")




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

default = default.copy()
default["default_yes"] = (default["default"] == "Yes").astype(int)

default_fit = smf.logit(
    "default_yes ~ C(student) + balance + income",
    data=default
).fit()

print(default_fit.summary())
print(np.exp(default_fit.params))
default["prob_default"] = default_fit.predict(default)




The fitted probabilities can be sorted, binned, and compared with observed default rates. This helps students see whether high predicted risk actually corresponds to higher observed risk.

title: 15  Classification Model Comparison
text:
15.4 Thresholds and Error Costs
Logistic regression returns probabilities. A threshold turns probabilities into class labels:

RPython



pred_class <- ifelse(Default$prob_default > 0.5, "Yes", "No")
table(predicted = pred_class, observed = Default$default)




pred_class = np.where(default["prob_default"] > 0.5, "Yes", "No")
print(pd.crosstab(pred_class, default["default"]))




The threshold should reflect the decision context. If false negatives are expensive, a lower threshold may be appropriate. If false positives are expensive, a higher threshold may be appropriate. The statistical model estimates risk; the threshold encodes a decision rule.

title: 15  Classification Model Comparison
text:
15.5 LDA and QDA Baselines
Discriminant analysis starts by modeling the distribution of predictors within each class. Bayes’ rule gives

\Pr(Y=k \mid X=x)
=
\frac{\pi_k f_k(x)}
{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K} \pi_\ell f_\ell(x)},

where \pi_k is the prior probability of class k and f_k(x) is the class-conditional density.
LDA assumes that each class has a multivariate normal predictor distribution with a common covariance matrix. This produces linear decision boundaries. QDA allows a different covariance matrix in each class, producing quadratic boundaries.

RPython



library(MASS)

lda_fit <- lda(default ~ balance + income + student, data = Default)
qda_fit <- qda(default ~ balance + income + student, data = Default)

lda_pred <- predict(lda_fit)$posterior[, "Yes"]
qda_pred <- predict(qda_fit)$posterior[, "Yes"]




from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X = default[["balance", "income", "student"]]
y = default["default"]

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("student", OneHotEncoder(drop="first"), ["student"])
], remainder="passthrough")

lda_fit = make_pipeline(preprocess, LinearDiscriminantAnalysis()).fit(X, y)
qda_fit = make_pipeline(preprocess, QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis()).fit(X, y)

lda_pred = lda_fit.predict_proba(X)[:, list(lda_fit.classes_).index("Yes")]
qda_pred = qda_fit.predict_proba(X)[:, list(qda_fit.classes_).index("Yes")]




LDA can be more stable when data are limited because it estimates fewer parameters. QDA can be more flexible when class covariance patterns really differ and there is enough data to estimate them.

title: 15  Classification Model Comparison
text:
15.6 ROC, AUC, and Calibration
Classification evaluation should include more than one number:







Measure
What it answers




Accuracy
What fraction of labels are correct at one threshold?


Sensitivity
What fraction of positives are detected?


Specificity
What fraction of negatives are correctly rejected?


ROC curve
How do sensitivity and specificity trade off across thresholds?


AUC
How well are positives ranked above negatives?


Calibration
Do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies?



ROC curves evaluate ranking across thresholds. Calibration evaluates probability quality. A model can rank well and still produce poorly calibrated probabilities.
