title: 16  Margins and Perceptron
text:
16.1 Learning Objectives
This chapter prepares for support vector machines by focusing on the geometry of linear classification. The central object is a decision boundary: a line, plane, or hyperplane that separates predicted classes.

title: 16  Margins and Perceptron
text:
Describe a linear classifier as a separating hyperplane.
Explain the perceptron update rule.
Define functional and geometric margins.
Connect margins to robustness and support vector machines.
Compare perceptron learning with logistic regression and linear margin-based classification.

title: 16  Margins and Perceptron
text:
16.2 Linear Decision Boundaries
For labels y_i \in \{-1,1\}, a linear classifier predicts with

\hat y_i = \operatorname{sign}(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta).

The boundary is the set of points where

\beta_0 + x^\top\beta = 0.

In two dimensions this is a line; in three dimensions it is a plane; in more dimensions it is a hyperplane. The coefficients determine the orientation of the boundary, and the intercept shifts it.

title: 16  Margins and Perceptron
text:
16.3 Perceptron Learning
The perceptron updates the boundary whenever it misclassifies an observation. Starting from initial weights w and intercept b, the prediction is

\hat y_i = \operatorname{sign}(w^\top x_i + b).

If observation i is misclassified, update

w \leftarrow w + \eta y_i x_i,
\qquad
b \leftarrow b + \eta y_i,

where \eta is a learning rate. The update moves the boundary in a direction that makes the current observation more likely to be classified correctly.

RPython



set.seed(571)
x1 <- rnorm(100)
x2 <- rnorm(100)
y <- ifelse(x1 + x2 + rnorm(100, sd = 0.5) > 0, 1, -1)
plot(x1, x2, col = ifelse(y == 1, "steelblue", "firebrick"), pch = 19)




import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
x1 = rng.normal(size=100)
x2 = rng.normal(size=100)
y = np.where(x1 + x2 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 100) > 0, 1, -1)

colors = np.where(y == 1, "steelblue", "firebrick")
plt.scatter(x1, x2, c=colors)
plt.xlabel("x1")
plt.ylabel("x2")
plt.show()




The perceptron is useful because it shows learning as geometry. It is not usually the final applied method in this course, but it motivates modern linear classifiers.

title: 16  Margins and Perceptron
text:
16.4 Margins
The margin measures how far an observation is from the decision boundary. Points near the boundary are fragile: a small perturbation can change their predicted class. Points far from the boundary are more stable.
The functional margin is

y_i(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta).

The geometric margin rescales by the coefficient norm:

\frac{y_i(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta)}{\|\beta\|}.

Maximizing the smallest geometric margin produces a classifier that separates the classes with the widest possible gap when perfect separation is available.

title: 16  Margins and Perceptron
text:
16.5 From Mistakes to Loss Functions
The perceptron responds only to mistakes. Logistic regression minimizes log loss and estimates probabilities. Support vector machines minimize hinge loss, which penalizes points inside the margin even when they are correctly classified:

\max\{0, 1 - y_i(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta)\}.

This loss encourages a boundary that is not merely correct, but correct with margin.

title: 16  Margins and Perceptron
text:
16.6 Boundary Comparison
A useful two-dimensional analysis compares three fitted boundaries:

perceptron boundary from iterative updates,
logistic regression boundary from probability modeling,
margin-based boundary from a linear support vector classifier.

The comparison should focus on the points closest to the boundary. Those points drive the distinction between a classifier that separates the data and a classifier that separates them robustly.

title: 17  Tree-Based Methods
text:
17.1 Learning Objectives
Tree-based methods partition the predictor space into regions and make simple predictions inside each region. A single tree is easy to explain and capable of representing interactions and nonlinearities, but it can be unstable. That instability motivates ensemble methods in the next chapter.

title: 17  Tree-Based Methods
text:
Explain recursive binary splitting.
Distinguish regression trees and classification trees.
Interpret impurity, tree depth, terminal nodes, and pruning.
Use cross-validation to choose tree complexity.
Compare a tree with a linear or logistic baseline.

title: 17  Tree-Based Methods
text:
17.2 Recursive Binary Splitting
A decision tree repeatedly splits the predictor space. At each step, it chooses a variable and cut point that best improve the fit.
For regression trees, a common objective is reduction in residual sum of squares. For classification trees, common impurity measures include the Gini index

G = \sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat p_{mk}(1-\hat p_{mk})

and cross-entropy

D = -\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat p_{mk}\log(\hat p_{mk}),

where \hat p_{mk} is the proportion of class k observations in node m.

title: 17  Tree-Based Methods
text:
17.3 Tree Structure
A fitted tree contains:







Term
Meaning




Root node
The full training data before any split


Internal node
A region that is split again


Terminal node
A final region used for prediction


Depth
Number of split levels from root to leaf


Split rule
A predictor threshold or category partition


Prediction
Mean response or class distribution inside a terminal node



Prediction follows a path of questions. This makes trees easy to communicate to nontechnical audiences.

title: 17  Tree-Based Methods
text:
17.4 Ames and Carseats Examples
In a housing example, a regression tree may split first on overall quality or living area, then on neighborhood, age, or basement size. In a car-seat sales example, a tree may split on shelving location, price, advertising, or competitor price.

RPython



library(rpart)

sales_tree <- rpart(Sales ~ ., data = ISLR::Carseats)
printcp(sales_tree)
plot(sales_tree)
text(sales_tree, use.n = TRUE)




import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, plot_tree
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X = carseats.drop(columns=["Sales"])
y = carseats["Sales"]
categorical = X.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical)
], remainder="passthrough")

sales_tree = make_pipeline(
    preprocess,
    DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=571, min_samples_leaf=10)
).fit(X, y)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plot_tree(sales_tree.named_steps["decisiontreeregressor"], max_depth=3)
plt.show()




The tree should be read as a set of local comparisons. A split near the root affects many observations; a split near a leaf affects a smaller subgroup.

title: 17  Tree-Based Methods
text:
17.5 Stopping and Pruning
A fully grown tree can overfit. Tree complexity can be controlled by minimum node size, maximum depth, minimum improvement, or cost-complexity pruning.
Cost-complexity pruning chooses a subtree by minimizing

\sum_{m=1}^{|T|} \sum_{i:x_i \in R_m}(y_i-\hat y_{R_m})^2
+ \alpha |T|.

The tuning parameter \alpha penalizes tree size. Larger values produce smaller trees.

RPython



best_cp <- sales_tree$cptable[
  which.min(sales_tree$cptable[, "xerror"]),
  "CP"
]
pruned_tree <- prune(sales_tree, cp = best_cp)




tree_model = sales_tree.named_steps["decisiontreeregressor"]
path = tree_model.cost_complexity_pruning_path(
    sales_tree.named_steps["columntransformer"].transform(X),
    y
)
ccp_alphas = path.ccp_alphas
print(ccp_alphas[:10])




Cross-validation should be used to choose the pruning level. A smaller tree with nearly the same error is often preferable because it is easier to explain and less sensitive to noise.

title: 17  Tree-Based Methods
text:
17.6 Strengths and Limits
Trees naturally capture:

nonlinear relationships,
interactions,
threshold effects,
mixed numeric and categorical predictors.

Their main weakness is variance. A small change in the training data can produce a different first split, which changes the whole tree. A single tree is therefore useful for interpretation and exploration, but not always the most accurate predictor.

text:

title: 18  Ensemble Methods
text:
18.1 Learning Objectives
Ensembles improve prediction by combining many models. A single tree can have high variance; bagging, random forests, and boosting use many trees to produce more accurate and stable predictions.

title: 18  Ensemble Methods
text:
Explain why averaging many models can reduce variance.
Compare bagging, random forests, and boosting.
Tune ensemble models using resampling.
Interpret variable importance and partial dependence with caution.
Evaluate whether extra accuracy is worth lower transparency.

title: 18  Ensemble Methods
text:
18.2 Averaging and Variance Reduction
If several predictors are unbiased and not perfectly correlated, averaging them can reduce variance. Bagging applies this idea to trees: fit many trees on bootstrap samples and average their predictions.
For regression,

\hat f_{\text{bag}}(x)
= \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat f^{*b}(x).

For classification, trees can vote or average class probabilities.

title: 18  Ensemble Methods
text:
18.3 Bagging
Bagging uses bootstrap samples to create many training sets. Each tree is usually grown deeply, so individual trees are flexible and unstable. The average is more stable than any one tree.

RPython



library(randomForest)

bag_fit <- randomForest(
  High ~ .,
  data = train,
  mtry = ncol(train) - 1,
  importance = TRUE
)




from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

bag_fit = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=500,
    max_features=None,
    random_state=571
)
bag_fit.fit(X_train, y_train)




When mtry equals the number of predictors, each split can consider all variables. This is bagging for tree models.

title: 18  Ensemble Methods
text:
18.4 Random Forests
Random forests modify bagging by allowing each split to consider only a random subset of predictors. This decorrelates the trees. If one predictor is very strong, ordinary bagging may use it near the top of many trees, making the trees similar. Random predictor selection gives other variables a chance to define different partitions.
Important tuning parameters include:



Parameter
Effect




Number of trees
More trees stabilize the average


mtry
Smaller values decorrelate trees more strongly


Node size
Controls depth and local flexibility


Sampling scheme
Affects class balance and bootstrap variation

title: 18  Ensemble Methods
text:
18.5 Boosting
Boosting builds an additive model sequentially:

\hat f(x) = \sum_{b=1}^{B}\lambda \hat f_b(x).

Each new tree focuses on structure that the current ensemble has not captured well. The learning rate \lambda controls how much each tree contributes. Smaller learning rates usually require more trees but can generalize better.

RPython



library(gbm)

boost_fit <- gbm(
  Sales ~ .,
  data = train,
  distribution = "gaussian",
  n.trees = 3000,
  interaction.depth = 3,
  shrinkage = 0.01,
  cv.folds = 5
)




from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor

boost_fit = GradientBoostingRegressor(
    n_estimators=3000,
    learning_rate=0.01,
    max_depth=3,
    random_state=571
)
boost_fit.fit(X_train, y_train)




Boosting is powerful, but it has more tuning choices: number of trees, learning rate, interaction depth, and minimum observations in terminal nodes.

title: 18  Ensemble Methods
text:
18.6 Comparing Tree Ensembles
A disciplined comparison uses the same split or resampling plan for all models:

fit a pruned single tree,
fit a bagged tree ensemble,
fit a random forest,
fit a boosted tree model,
tune only inside training folds,
evaluate the selected models on held-out data.

The comparison should include both predictive performance and the cost of complexity.

title: 18  Ensemble Methods
text:
18.7 Interpretation
Ensembles are less transparent than single trees, but several summaries help:








Tool
Use
Caution




Variable importance
Ranks influential predictors
Can be biased by scale or cardinality


Partial dependence
Shows average fitted effect
Can be misleading with strong interactions


Individual conditional curves
Shows heterogeneity across observations
Can be crowded and noisy


Test performance
Measures generalization
Does not explain the model alone



Interpretation should be tied to the fitted model and the data distribution, not treated as a causal explanation.

title: 19  Support Vector Machines
text:
19.1 Learning Objectives
Support vector machines use margins and kernels to construct classifiers that can be linear in a transformed feature space while nonlinear in the original variables.

title: 19  Support Vector Machines
text:
Explain maximal-margin and soft-margin classification.
Interpret support vectors and the cost parameter.
Compare linear, polynomial, and radial kernels.
Explain why scaling is essential for SVMs.
Tune cost and kernel parameters with cross-validation.

title: 19  Support Vector Machines
text:
19.2 Separating Hyperplanes
For classes coded as y_i \in \{-1,1\}, a separating hyperplane has the form

f(x) = \beta_0 + x^\top\beta.

The predicted class is the sign of f(x). If the classes are perfectly separable, many hyperplanes may classify the training data correctly. The maximal-margin classifier chooses the hyperplane with the largest distance to the closest training points.
Those closest points are the support vectors. They determine the boundary; observations far from the boundary do not directly control the fit.

title: 19  Support Vector Machines
text:
19.3 Soft Margins
Perfect separation is rare and can lead to overly sensitive boundaries. The soft-margin classifier allows violations:

y_i(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta) \geq 1 - \xi_i,
\qquad \xi_i \geq 0.

The cost parameter controls the penalty for violations. A large cost allows fewer violations and may produce a narrower margin. A small cost allows more violations and may produce a wider, more stable margin.

RPython



library(e1071)

linear_svm <- svm(
  class ~ .,
  data = train,
  kernel = "linear",
  cost = 1,
  scale = TRUE
)




from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC

linear_svm = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    SVC(kernel="linear", C=1)
)
linear_svm.fit(X_train, y_train)

title: 19  Support Vector Machines
text:
19.4 Kernels
Kernels compute similarity after an implicit feature transformation. This allows nonlinear boundaries without explicitly creating all transformed variables.








Kernel
Form
Boundary behavior




Linear
x_i^\top x_j
Linear in original predictors


Polynomial
(c + x_i^\top x_j)^d
Global curved boundaries


Radial basis
\exp(-\gamma\|x_i-x_j\|^2)
Local flexible boundaries



The radial kernel is often effective because it can create local nonlinear boundaries. Its flexibility depends on \gamma: larger values create more local influence.

title: 19  Support Vector Machines
text:
19.5 Iris Decision Surfaces
A two-feature iris classification example makes kernels visible. Fit linear, polynomial, and radial SVMs on the same scaled predictors, then plot the predicted class across a grid. The linear kernel creates a straight boundary in the two-dimensional plot. The polynomial and radial kernels can bend around class structure.

RPython



tuned <- tune(
  svm,
  class ~ .,
  data = train,
  kernel = "radial",
  ranges = list(cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = c(0.1, 1, 5))
)

best_svm <- tuned$best.model




from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC

svm_pipeline = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="rbf"))
tuned = GridSearchCV(
    svm_pipeline,
    param_grid={
        "svc__C": [0.1, 1, 10],
        "svc__gamma": [0.1, 1, 5]
    },
    cv=5
)
tuned.fit(X_train, y_train)
best_svm = tuned.best_estimator_




This comparison should emphasize that better visual separation on the training data is not enough. Kernel choice and tuning parameters must be chosen with validation or cross-validation.

title: 19  Support Vector Machines
text:
19.6 Scaling and Tuning
SVMs depend on distances and inner products, so feature scale matters. If one predictor has a much larger numeric range than another, it can dominate the margin and kernel values.
The usual tuning sequence is:

split the data,
center and scale predictors inside the training data,
choose candidate kernels,
tune cost and kernel-specific parameters by cross-validation,
evaluate the selected model on held-out data,
inspect support vectors and decision surfaces where possible.

title: 20  Unsupervised Learning
text:
20.1 Learning Objectives
Unsupervised learning searches for structure without a designated response variable. Because there is no outcome to predict, the quality of the analysis depends on preprocessing, distance measures, stability, and whether the discovered structure answers a meaningful question.

title: 20  Unsupervised Learning
text:
Distinguish supervised prediction from unsupervised structure discovery.
Use PCA for visualization and compression.
Compare k-means and hierarchical clustering.
Explain how scaling and distance metrics affect clusters.
Evaluate unsupervised results with stability and interpretability.

title: 20  Unsupervised Learning
section: 20.2 No Response, No Single Test Error
text:
20.2 No Response, No Single Test Error
In supervised learning, held-out error provides a natural evaluation target. In unsupervised learning, there is no response variable, so there is no single test error to optimize. Instead, analysts ask:

Are the patterns stable under reasonable preprocessing choices?
Are clusters separated enough to describe?
Do the patterns persist across resamples?
Are the discovered groups useful for a later scientific or business question?
Could the result be an artifact of scale, outliers, or distance choice?

title: 20  Unsupervised Learning
text:
20.3 PCA for Structure
PCA is often used to visualize high-dimensional data before clustering. It creates uncorrelated component scores ordered by explained variance.

RPython



x <- scale(USArrests)
pca <- prcomp(x)
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], pch = 19)




from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = StandardScaler().fit_transform(us_arrests)
pca = PCA().fit_transform(x)

plt.scatter(pca[:, 0], pca[:, 1])
plt.xlabel("PC1")
plt.ylabel("PC2")
plt.show()




The first two components may reveal broad separation among observations, but they do not guarantee meaningful clusters. PCA finds directions of high variance, not necessarily directions that match a substantive grouping.

title: 20  Unsupervised Learning
text:
20.4 K-Means Clustering
K-means partitions observations into K clusters by minimizing within-cluster squared distance:

\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in C_k}\|x_i-\bar x_k\|^2.


RPython



set.seed(571)
km3 <- kmeans(x, centers = 3, nstart = 20)
km3$cluster




from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

km3 = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=20, random_state=571).fit(x)
print(km3.labels_)




The analyst chooses K. Common aids include within-cluster sum of squares, silhouette summaries, stability checks, and interpretability of cluster profiles. None of these automatically proves the “true” number of clusters.

title: 20  Unsupervised Learning
text:
20.5 Hierarchical Clustering
Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of nested groupings. It requires a distance metric and linkage rule.

RPython



hc_complete <- hclust(dist(x), method = "complete")
plot(hc_complete)
rect.hclust(hc_complete, k = 3)




from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, fcluster, linkage
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hc_complete = linkage(x, method="complete")
dendrogram(hc_complete)
plt.show()
clusters = fcluster(hc_complete, t=3, criterion="maxclust")




Complete linkage tends to create compact clusters. Single linkage can chain observations together. Average linkage is often a middle ground. Changing linkage can change the dendrogram, so the choice should be reported.

title: 20  Unsupervised Learning
text:
20.6 Scaling and Distance
Clustering is often dominated by scale. If one variable has a much larger numeric range, Euclidean distance will emphasize that variable. Standardization is common, but it is not automatic truth. Scaling says that one standard deviation in each variable should count equally.
Outliers also matter. A small number of unusual observations can affect cluster centers, dendrogram structure, and PCA directions. The opening analysis should therefore include summaries, plots, and sensitivity checks.

title: 20  Unsupervised Learning
text:
20.7 Cluster Profiles
Clusters become useful when they can be described. After assigning clusters, summarize original variables by cluster:

RPython



aggregate(USArrests, by = list(cluster = km3$cluster), mean)




profiles = us_arrests.assign(cluster=km3.labels_).groupby("cluster").mean()
print(profiles)




Profiles should be written in the original measurement units when possible. A cluster label is not an explanation; it is a concise name for a pattern that must be interpreted in context.

Scale a numeric data set, visualize the first two principal component scores, run k-means for several values of K, and compare with hierarchical clustering under at least two linkage rules. Report cluster profiles, stability checks, and a cautious interpretation of what the groups do and do not imply.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
21.1 Learning Objectives
The final chapter brings the course together around reproducible analysis, communication, model limitations, and responsible use. A good statistical learning project is not a list of fitted models. It is a defensible workflow from question to data to evidence to decision.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
Describe a complete statistical learning workflow.
Communicate model performance, uncertainty, and limitations.
Identify reproducibility risks in notebooks and ad hoc analyses.
Compare models using evidence matched to the project goal.
Connect classical statistical learning habits to modern machine learning practice.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
21.2 The Complete Workflow
A complete project should make each of these choices visible:

research or prediction question,
observational unit and response variable,
candidate predictors and data exclusions,
preprocessing and feature engineering,
train/validation/test design,
candidate model classes,
tuning strategy,
final evaluation,
interpretation and uncertainty,
limitations and maintenance plan.

The workflow matters because most modeling failures are not caused by a single bad algorithm. They are caused by unclear targets, leakage, unstable preprocessing, poorly matched evaluation metrics, or overconfident interpretation.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
21.3 Choosing Evidence
Different goals require different evidence:







Goal
Evidence to emphasize




Accurate prediction
Held-out error, calibration, robustness


Explanation
Coefficients, uncertainty, diagnostics, design limitations


Screening
Sensitivity, specificity, threshold costs


Ranking
ROC/AUC, precision-recall, lift


Segmentation
Cluster stability, profiles, external validity


Communication
Simplicity, visuals, reproducibility



The final model should be justified using the evidence that matches the goal, not the metric that makes the model look best.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
21.4 Simulation as Practice
Monte Carlo simulation complements predictive modeling by propagating uncertainty through a decision model. Instead of reporting one static outcome, simulation reports a distribution of possible outcomes.

RPython



simulate_profit <- function(n, price, unit_cost, demand_mean, demand_sd) {
  demand <- pmax(0, rnorm(n, mean = demand_mean, sd = demand_sd))
  revenue <- price * demand
  cost <- unit_cost * demand
  revenue - cost
}

set.seed(571)
profit <- simulate_profit(
  n = 10000,
  price = 40,
  unit_cost = 25,
  demand_mean = 1000,
  demand_sd = 150
)

quantile(profit, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))




import numpy as np

def simulate_profit(n, price, unit_cost, demand_mean, demand_sd, seed=571):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    demand = np.maximum(0, rng.normal(demand_mean, demand_sd, n))
    revenue = price * demand
    cost = unit_cost * demand
    return revenue - cost

profit = simulate_profit(
    n=10000,
    price=40,
    unit_cost=25,
    demand_mean=1000,
    demand_sd=150
)

print(np.quantile(profit, [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]))




Simulation does not remove uncertainty. It makes uncertainty visible enough to reason about tradeoffs, tail outcomes, and risk tolerance.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
21.5 Reproducible Reporting
A reproducible report should allow another analyst to rerun the work and understand the decisions. It should include:

package versions or computing environment,
data source and cleaning rules,
random seeds for resampling,
train/test split definition,
model formulas or tuning grids,
final evaluation code,
clear tables and figures,
limitations written in ordinary language.

Reproducibility is also a communication practice. A reader should be able to distinguish observed data patterns, modeling assumptions, validation evidence, and recommendations.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
21.6 Responsible Interpretation
Models can encode bias, fail under distribution shift, and invite overconfident decisions. A final report should state:

what population the data represent,
what cases are excluded or underrepresented,
whether the task is predictive or causal,
which errors are most costly,
where the model should not be used,
how performance should be monitored over time.

Responsible statistical learning means treating a model as an evidence-producing tool, not as an authority.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
21.7 Final Project Structure
A strong final project uses the following structure:

question and motivation,
data description,
exploratory analysis,
preprocessing and splitting,
candidate models,
validation results,
final model and held-out evaluation,
interpretation,
limitations,
conclusion.

The conclusion should be short and specific: what was learned, how strong the evidence is, and what decision or next analysis follows.

title: 21  Statistical Learning in Practice
text:
21.8 Chapter Synthesis
Revise a complete modeling project into a reproducible report. Make the target, data construction, preprocessing, model comparison, final evaluation, and limitations explicit. The final product should read as a coherent analysis rather than a transcript of code execution.

title: 22  Applied Statistical Learning Case Studies
text:
22.2 Size Limits and Reproductive Contribution
A fishery management question might ask whether smaller mature fish contribute meaningfully to local replenishment, even when policy rules focus on larger fish. The statistical workflow is not a single model. It includes data cleaning, length conversion, distribution summaries, assignment probabilities, and uncertainty.
Key modeling tasks include:

define the population and sampling frame,
convert measurements onto a common length scale,
compare size distributions across management zones,
estimate reproductive contribution by size class,
summarize uncertainty with confidence intervals or simulation,
translate the result into a policy-relevant statement.

title: 22  Applied Statistical Learning Case Studies
text:
22.3 Distribution-Fitting Frame
Distribution fitting is useful when the goal is to describe a size, waiting-time, abundance, or loss distribution.

RPython



set.seed(571)
fish <- data.frame(
  length_cm = rgamma(500, shape = 9, scale = 4.2),
  zone = sample(c("fished", "reserve"), 500, replace = TRUE)
)

by(fish$length_cm, fish$zone, summary)
fit_gamma <- MASS::fitdistr(fish$length_cm, densfun = "gamma")
fit_gamma




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
fish = pd.DataFrame({
    "length_cm": rng.gamma(shape=9, scale=4.2, size=500),
    "zone": rng.choice(["fished", "reserve"], size=500)
})

print(fish.groupby("zone")["length_cm"].describe())
shape, loc, scale = stats.gamma.fit(fish["length_cm"], floc=0)
print({"shape": shape, "scale": scale})




The fitted distribution should be checked against the observed data. Goodness-of-fit summaries are evidence, not guarantees.

title: 22  Applied Statistical Learning Case Studies
text:
22.4 Simulation for Decision Support
Simulation can propagate uncertainty from biological or operational inputs into a policy-relevant quantity.

RPython



set.seed(571)
simulate_contribution <- function(n, mean_small, mean_large) {
  small <- rgamma(n, shape = 25, rate = 25 / mean_small)
  large <- rgamma(n, shape = 25, rate = 25 / mean_large)
  small / (small + large)
}

share_small <- simulate_contribution(10000, mean_small = 36, mean_large = 64)
quantile(share_small, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))




import numpy as np

def simulate_contribution(n, mean_small, mean_large, seed=571):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    small = rng.gamma(shape=25, scale=mean_small / 25, size=n)
    large = rng.gamma(shape=25, scale=mean_large / 25, size=n)
    return small / (small + large)

share_small = simulate_contribution(10000, mean_small=36, mean_large=64)
print(np.quantile(share_small, [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]))




The simulation does not settle the policy question by itself. It makes the consequences of assumptions visible and gives the analyst a way to describe uncertainty in the decision quantity.
